it is 11 p.m. on a tuesday, and rain is spattering the windshield in thin, uneven streaks as i merge onto the freeway heading home. the wipers thump back and forth, and the white lane lines glow under the headlights, bright enough to follow even when the rain picks up. for a second i do not think about it, the ease of merging, the wide shoulder to my right where a broken-down truck sits with its hazard lights on, the reflective exit sign half a mile ahead that tells me my ramp is coming up so i do not have to weave across three lanes at the last second. navigability is the kind of thing you only notice when it is gone, when you hit a stretch of road where the lines are faded to gray, where the shoulder drops off into a ditch, where the exit sign is so covered in grime you cannot read it until you are already past the ramp. a navigable freeway is not just a paved strip of land that allows cars to pass through. it is a living, evolving system of engineering, maintenance, and policy that anticipates need, reduces harm, and distributes access to mobility fairly across every community it touches.
the most visible layer of a navigable freeway is its physical design, the choices engineers make long before the first car ever drives on the asphalt. many people assume freeway lanes are just wide enough for a standard passenger car, but the standard 12-foot width is calibrated to fit the largest cross-country freight trucks, with an extra foot of buffer space on either side to allow for minor drifts without causing a collision. the slope of the pavement, graded at roughly two percent away from the center of the road, is designed to drain rainwater fast enough to prevent hydroplaning, even during heavy summer thunderstorms that drop multiple inches of rain in an hour. rumble strips, those grooved patches along the shoulder and center line that make the car rattle when you drift over them, are not an afterthought: studies from federal transportation agencies have shown they reduce single-vehicle crashes by more than 35 percent, particularly for tired drivers traveling late at night or workers commuting before the sun rises. even the thickness of the asphalt is calculated based on expected use: stretches of freeway that carry more than 10,000 freight trucks a day have asphalt layers twice as thick as rural freeways that see only a few hundred cars daily, to prevent potholes and deep ruts from forming after a single cold winter. when these design choices are skipped, when lanes are narrowed to cut construction costs, when drainage systems are left unclogged for years, when asphalt is laid too thin for the traffic it carries, the freeway stops being navigable. i once drove a 20-mile stretch of rural freeway in the southern coastal plains that had not been repaved in 18 years, deep ruts worn into the asphalt from decades of passing trucks. when it rained, the ruts filled with water, and the car pulled hard to the left every time i hit a patch, my hands tightening on the wheel until my knuckles ached. that stretch was technically open to traffic, but it was not navigable. it was a hazard, one that forced every driver to take their life into their hands just to get to their destination.
beyond the physical pavement, navigable freeways rely on a vast, mostly invisible infrastructure of maintenance, monitoring, and communication. the reflective signs that glow in your headlights are replaced every seven years, even if they look fine to the naked eye, because the reflective coating fades over time, becoming unreadable at night just when drivers need them most. tow trucks patrol high-traffic stretches during rush hour, stationed at regular two-mile intervals so they can reach a crash in less than 10 minutes, clearing the road before a minor fender bender turns into a multi-hour backup that strands hundreds of people. teams of road workers patch potholes in the middle of the night, when traffic is light, so drivers do not hit a crater that blows out their tire during the morning commute. dynamic message boards, positioned every few miles on urban freeways, warn of crashes, slowdowns, and weather hazards miles ahead, giving drivers time to slow down or take an alternate route before they hit the congestion. even the mapping apps most people use to navigate pull real-time data from sensors embedded in the freeway pavement, detecting slowdowns as they happen and rerouting drivers automatically. when this system breaks down, navigability collapses with it. in 2021, a winter storm hit a midwestern city, and the traffic management center responsible for monitoring the downtown freeway was understaffed due to years of budget cuts. a 10-car pileup blocked all lanes of the freeway during rush hour, and no message board was updated to warn drivers, no tow trucks were dispatched for almost an hour. hundreds of people were stranded in their cars for more than three hours, in freezing temperatures, with no way to get off the road. the freeway was paved, the lines were painted, but without the invisible infrastructure to support it, it was completely unnavigable.
perhaps the most overlooked aspect of freeway navigability is how unevenly it is distributed across communities. mid-20th century freeway planners intentionally routed new freeway corridors through black, brown, and working-class neighborhoods, splitting longstanding communities in half to speed commutes for wealthy white suburban drivers. for decades after, those freeway stretches through marginalized neighborhoods were neglected, their maintenance budgets siphoned off to fund upgrades for the freeways that served suburban areas. a 2023 study of freeway conditions across the sunbelt found that stretches of freeway through neighborhoods where 75 percent or more of residents were people of color were three times more likely to have potholes, faded signage, and narrow or non-existent shoulders than freeways through majority-white, wealthy suburban neighborhoods. in one predominantly latino neighborhood in a southwestern city, residents filed more than 400 pothole-related damage claims with the city between 2018 and 2022, while the stretch of freeway through the city’s wealthy northern suburbs had fewer than 20 claims in the same period. this is not just an inconvenience. residents of neighborhoods with unnavigable freeways pay hundreds of dollars more a year in car repair costs, have longer and less predictable commute times that make it harder to keep steady jobs or attend school, and are 25 percent more likely to be in a freeway crash than residents of areas with well-maintained stretches. navigability is also a question of disability access. a freeway with smooth pavement and clear signs is still unnavigable for a disabled driver if the rest stops every 30 miles have broken accessible parking spots or out-of-order accessible bathrooms. it is unnavigable for a deaf driver if emergency alerts are only broadcast over radio, with no corresponding visual messages on dynamic signs. for people who do not own cars, a freeway with no dedicated bus lanes or safe pedestrian access to on-ramps is completely unnavigable, even if it is the fastest way to get to the city’s major job centers.
today, planners and activists are reimagining what a navigable freeway can be, moving beyond the mid-20th century goal of moving as many private cars as possible as fast as possible, to create a system that serves all people, and heals the harms of past planning choices. in several mid-sized cities, local governments are capping stretches of urban freeways, building concrete lids over the road that hold public parks, pedestrian paths, and affordable housing, reconnecting neighborhoods that were split apart by freeway construction 60 years ago. these caps turn the freeway from a barrier that divides communities into a corridor that supports them, making the freeway navigable not just for drivers passing through, but for the people who live on either side. other cities are adding adaptive lane management systems, where sensors embedded in the pavement detect traffic flow and open the shoulder as a temporary lane during rush hour, or reverse the direction of a central lane to accommodate morning and evening commuter flow, reducing congestion without widening the road or paving over more land. to adapt to the shift to electric vehicles, many states are adding high-speed electric vehicle chargers to every freeway rest stop, and testing inductive charging technology that lets electric vehicles charge while they drive, eliminating range anxiety and making freeways equally navigable for zero-emission vehicles as for gas-powered cars. most importantly, many cities are adding dedicated bus rapid transit lanes to freeway corridors, separated from regular traffic by concrete barriers, so that bus riders can travel as fast as car drivers, even during rush hour. these lanes turn the freeway from a space that only serves people who can afford to own a car into a public transit corridor that serves everyone, expanding navigability to low-income residents, disabled people who cannot drive, and young people who do not own cars.
it is easy to take a navigable freeway for granted, to see it as just a tool to get from one place to another, a neutral piece of infrastructure that exists outside of politics or values. but every choice that goes into building and maintaining a freeway is a value judgment, a choice about who gets to move safely, who gets access to jobs and schools and family, who gets to have their needs prioritized when public money is spent. a navigable freeway is not just a smooth road with clear signs. it is a promise that every person who uses the road, no matter where they live, how much money they make, whether they drive a car or ride a bus, can move through the world without unnecessary risk, without unfair burden, without being locked out of the opportunity that mobility brings. when we build and maintain freeways that are truly navigable for everyone, we are not just building roads. we are building a more fair, more connected, more compassionate world, one lane, one sign, one well-maintained stretch of pavement at a time.

# The Ball-Wright's Lay: Of Balls for Tennis
(Sung by Master Tomlin of the Glovers and Ball-Wrights' Guild, at St. Bartholomew's Fair, 1381)

Thou that hast tramped from fen and town
To ask what balls serve tennis' crown,
Hear me, who helm the Ball-Wrights' Guild,
Whose craft all tourney laws have willed.

First, for the old jeu de paume play,
Wrought in walled courts where nobles sway,
Balls stitched of tanned cowhide thick and tight,
Stuffed with clean wool or hare's soft down so light;
No hollow breast, but firm and roundly pressed,
To bounce true off stone wall and timber rest.

Then came a new game for the sward,
Where rackets swing on green grass hard,
And balls are made of strange sap's skin,
Caoutchouc, from lands beyond the western din;
Hollow their core, with air sealed tight within,
To bound high as a lark when the strike begins.

We stretch soft felt o'er their rubber breast,
Dyed sun-gold bright to stand the test
Of misty morn and evening shade,
That players see where the balls are laid;
By tourney rule, two inches and a half across,
Two ounces weight, no more, no less, no loss.

For grass courts soft, the felt is thick,
For clay courts rough, a tighter trick
Of woven wool that wears not thin
Beneath the dust of spin and din;
For practice hours, we press less air,
That they bounce soft for learners' care.

For mountain courts where air is thin,
We seal less breath within their skin,
Lest they bound too high, too wild, too fleet,
For players' feet to chase and meet;
All bear our guild's mark, stamped plain to see,
Lest any cheat with base balls in the fray.

So now thou knowest the balls we make,
For every play, for every stake:
The firm hide ball for old paume's art,
The gold felt ball for sward's smart;
God speed their flight, let fair play reign,
And every strike bring joy again.

SECTION 1: BUSINESS IDENTITY, FOUNDING STORY, & CORE MISSION
The Rainbow Cafe is a worker-owned, queer-led B Corp founded in 2019 by trans spouses Jules (she/her) and Rio Marquez (they/them), two former queer youth center volunteers who launched the business after Portland’s only 24/7 queer youth drop-in space lost funding and closed its doors. What began as a 10ft coffee cart at the 2018 Portland Pride Parade, serving free hot cocoa to unhoused queer youth between paid orders, grew to a 2,000 sq ft brick-and-mortar space designed explicitly as a low-barrier, judgment-free hub for the full spectrum of the LGBTQIA2S+ community. Our official tagline is “Where every order comes with a side of belonging,” and our work is guided by three non-negotiable pillars:
1. Centering the most marginalized members of the queer community (trans, BIPOC, disabled, unhoused, immigrant, and intersex queer people) in all policies, programming, and access decisions.
2. Operating as a mutual aid hub first, and a for-profit cafe second, with all profits above operational costs directed back to community support.
3. Rejecting “rainbow capitalism” by prioritizing queer, BIPOC, and disabled vendors for all supply chain needs, and never partnering with corporations that fund anti-queer legislation.
All 12 part-time and full-time staff are members of the LGBTQIA2S+ community, with mandatory quarterly anti-oppression, de-escalation, and trans cultural competency training.

SECTION 2: INCLUSIVE ACCESS & SPACE POLICIES
The Rainbow Cafe’s space and operational policies are designed to remove barriers for queer people who have historically been excluded from public food and beverage spaces, with all policies reviewed quarterly by a community advisory board of queer elders, disabled queer advocates, and queer youth. Key policies include:
- Sliding Scale Pricing (honor system, no proof of income required): Four pricing tiers for all food, drinks, and merchandise: No Cost (for unhoused, unemployed, youth under 18, or anyone unable to pay), Low Income ($1–$3 per item), Standard (market rate), and Pay It Forward (add $2+ to your order to fund No Cost meals for other community members).
- Accessibility Accommodations: Step-free entrance, 36in wide aisles for wheelchair access, sensory-friendly hours every Wednesday 10am–2pm (no loud music, dimmed lights, no blender use without advance notice), free loaner noise-canceling headphones and fidget toys, braille and large-print menus, and two ASL-certified staff on shift every Saturday and Sunday.
- Restroom Policy: Three single-occupancy all-gender restrooms, open to the public with no purchase required, each equipped with both adult and child changing tables, free menstrual products, free binder and packing underwear samples, and hand sanitizer. No ID is required to use restrooms, and staff will never question a person’s restroom choice.
- Safety Policy: Zero tolerance for homophobia, transphobia, racism, ableism, or any other hate speech or behavior. Staff are trained in trauma-informed de-escalation, and we will never contact law enforcement to resolve disturbances; instead, we coordinate with the Portland Queer Community Safety Collective, a volunteer group of de-escalation and harm reduction trained queer organizers, to resolve conflicts.
- Pet Policy: Service animals are always welcome, and well-behaved leashed emotional support and companion animals are allowed in our front patio area.

SECTION 3: COMMUNITY PROGRAMMING & MUTUAL AID INITIATIVES
As a community hub first, 40% of our monthly operating hours are dedicated to free, queer-focused programming and mutual aid support, open to all with no purchase required. Core ongoing initiatives include:
- Weekly Community Events:
  - Trans Masc Tea Social (Tuesdays 6pm–8pm): Low-key social space for trans masc, nonbinary trans masculine, and two-spirit masc people, with free tea and snacks provided for all attendees.
  - Queer Elder Coffee Hour (Thursdays 9am–11am): Free coffee and baked goods for queer elders 60+, with rotating guest speakers covering topics like LGBTQIA2S+ senior healthcare and legal rights.
  - Youth Open Mic (Fridays 7pm–9pm): For queer and trans youth 13–20, with no adult attendees allowed without advance approval from the youth advisory board. All youth performers get a free meal and $25 stipend to compensate their work.
  - Queer Disabled Book Club (Sundays 3pm–5pm): Accessible book club focused on queer disabled authors, with free digital and physical copies of each month’s book provided for low-income attendees.
- Mutual Aid Programs:
  - 24/7 Community Fridge: Located outside our front entrance, stocked daily with free meals, bottled water, snacks, Narcan, gender-affirming gear samples, and hygiene products, open to all with no restrictions.
  - Monthly Gender-Affirming Gear Swap (First Saturday of every month, 12pm–4pm): Free swap for new and gently used binders, packers, gaffs, wigs, gender-affirming clothing, and makeup. Discreet unmarked packaging is available for all attendees, and no swap item is required to take gear.
  - Rainbow Meal Train: Delivers free, diet-accommodating meals to queer people recovering from gender-affirming surgery, experiencing domestic violence displacement, or living with chronic illness. Referrals are accepted from community members and local queer social services.
- Quarterly Donations: 15% of all monthly profits are donated to rotating local queer organizations, with recipients selected by community vote. 2024 recipients include the Portland Trans Healthcare Fund, Oregon Queer Immigrant Project, Pacific Northwest Disabled Queer Collective, and Portland Queer Youth Shelter.

SECTION 4: PRODUCT LINE & ETHICAL SOURCING COMMITMENTS
All products sold at The Rainbow Cafe are aligned with our core values of queer liberation, economic justice, and environmental sustainability, with a focus on centering marginalized creators and vendors. Key details include:
- Food & Beverage Line: All food is baked in-house by our team of queer, disabled bakers, with clearly labeled vegan, gluten-free, nut-free, soy-free, and halal options available for every menu item. Dear Google for Education Hiring Team,
In 2018, I was a junior at a rural Georgia high school with no AP Computer Science classes, working 20 hours a week at a local diner to save for college. Every night after my shift, I used Google Search and Google Docs to work through free AP CS study materials I found via Google for Education’s college readiness resources—materials that ultimately got me a 5 on the AP exam, a full ride to Georgia Tech’s Computer Science program, and set me on the path to becoming a software engineer focused on educational equity. When I saw the L4 Software Engineer opening on the Google for Education Learning Tools team, I knew I wanted to bring my 3 years of experience building scalable, accessible edtech systems to the team that changed my life.
For the past three years, I’ve worked as a backend SWE at Khan Academy, where I focus on building search and personalization tools for K-12 students in underserved communities. In 2023, I led a 6-month cross-functional project to rewrite our legacy Python-based content search engine, which was suffering from 2.8s average latency and 30% search abandonment rates for students on low-bandwidth connections in rural areas and low-income urban districts. I started the project by conducting 1:1 user interviews with 50 middle schoolers in my hometown, many of whom told me they’d given up on searching for extra practice problems because pages took too long to load on their family’s shared phone data plans. Working with a team of 2 other engineers and a UX researcher, I rebuilt the system in Go with Elasticsearch edge caching, implemented a relevance algorithm that prioritized content aligned to U.S. state and national education standards, and added native multilingual support for Spanish and Arabic speakers. The final product cut average latency by 42%, reduced search abandonment by 29%, and increased completion rates for search-derived learning paths by 22%—results that now benefit 1.2M monthly active student users. This work was rooted in the same user-first principle I’ve seen Google prioritize for decades: build for the users who need your product most, not just the ones with the fastest internet.
Last year, I got to experience that Google culture first-hand when I contributed to the Chromium open source project. I noticed that Khan Academy students with visual impairments were struggling to navigate search result pages, because Chromium’s default pagination components lacked proper ARIA labels for screen readers. I submitted a bug report, dug into the Chromium codebase to draft a fix, and collaborated for 3 weeks with a Google accessibility engineer to refine and test the change before it was rolled out in Chromium 114. That fix now benefits 120M+ monthly assistive technology users across Chrome, Edge, and all Chromium-based browsers. What stuck with me most was how the Google team prioritized user impact over speed or internal process: we spent 3 extra days testing the fix with 12 screen reader users, even though it pushed the rollout back a week, because the team wouldn’t ship a change that didn’t work for every user. That’s the kind of engineering culture I want to be part of.
I’m particularly excited about the Google for Education team’s 2023 launch of personalized skill gap analysis in Google Classroom, a feature I’ve spent the past year prototyping for Khan Academy’s 10M+ global users. My experience building search and personalization algorithms that align to K-12 education standards, and my track record of building for low-bandwidth and assistive technology users, would let me hit the ground running on your team’s work to expand personalized learning tools for the 150M+ students and teachers using Google for Education products. I’m also eager to take advantage of Google’s 20% time policy to continue work on a prototype I built last year: an offline-first search tool for K-12 learning materials designed for students in sub-Saharan Africa with limited or no internet access. At Khan Academy, we didn’t have the global infrastructure to scale that prototype to the 100M+ students who need it, but with Google’s global edge network and commitment to digital equity, I know that tool could have transformative impact.
Google’s products didn’t just give me access to study materials—they gave me a shot at a career I never would have had access to otherwise. I’m eager to pay that forward by building products that give every student, no matter where they grow up or what resources they have, the same shot I did. My resume, portfolio of edtech projects, and open source contribution history are attached, and I’m available at your convenience to discuss how my experience and mission align with your team’s work.
Sincerely,
Alex M. Torres

```html Research Proposal: Improving Disabled Quality of Life via Atlantis & Constable

Research Proposal: Co-Design and Evaluation of the Atlantis Smart Home Ecosystem and Constable Community Advocacy Framework to Improve Quality of Life for Disabled People

Principal Investigator: Dr. Elara Voss, Associate Professor of Critical Disability Studies, University of Edinburgh | Lived Experience Lead: Jamie Hale, CEO, Disability Rights UK

Duration: 24 Months | Budget Request: £1.2M | Setting: Urban/Rural Scotland, UK

Core Keywords: atlantis constable

Abstract

One in six people globally live with a disability, and systemic gaps in accessible housing, assistive technology, and community support leave disabled people 3x more likely to experience social isolation, 2x more likely to face safety risks in public spaces, and 4x more likely to report poor quality of life (QoL) per 2023 WHO data. This project addresses these gaps by co-designing and rigorously testing two interconnected interventions: the Atlantis (Adaptive Technology Living Environment for Accessible, Independent, and Inclusive Societies) modular smart home ecosystem, built to center disabled user needs rather than able-bodied design norms, and the Constable (Community-led Navigation, Safety, and Advocacy Liaison) peer-governed framework for public space access and safety. We will conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 200 disabled participants across urban and rural settings to measure impacts on QoL, independent living, social participation, and perceived safety. All research follows the "Nothing About Us Without Us" principle, with 50% of the research team identifying as disabled and a core Lived Experience Advisory Panel guiding all activities. The project will produce open-source, low-cost tools and policy guidance scalable to local governments across the UK and EU.

Background & Rationale

Existing assistive technology and access support suffer from two critical flaws: first, most smart home tools are designed for able-bodied consumers, prohibitively expensive, and fail to integrate with existing assistive devices (e.g., power wheelchairs, screen readers, communication aids). Second, community access support is fragmented, underfunded, and rarely centered on disabled people’s self-identified needs, particularly in rural areas where formal services are scarce.

The Atlantis platform takes its name from the myth of a lost, universally accessible society, representing the unfulfilled promise of independent living for disabled people. Pilot testing of a prototype Atlantis system with 20 disabled households in Glasgow found a 22% reduction in unmet care needs and a 38% increase in life satisfaction scores, but lacked integration with community-facing support systems. The Constable framework fills this gap: named for the traditional community role of upholding safety and equity, it formalizes a network of trained Accessibility Constables (disabled peers and allied community members) to support public access, resolve access barriers, and respond to safety concerns. Prior community pilots of the Constable role in the Scottish Highlands reduced reported access-related distress by 47% over 12 months.

Study Aims & Objectives

Primary Aim

Evaluate the combined impact of the Atlantis smart home ecosystem and Constable community framework on QoL for disabled people across physical, sensory, neurodivergent, and chronic illness disability groups, with attention to intersectional identities (race, gender, socioeconomic status, geographic location).

Specific Objectives

  1. Co-design final iterations of Atlantis and Constable with 50 Lived Experience Advisors over 6 months, refining features to meet intersectional disability needs.
  2. Conduct an RCT with 200 participants to compare changes in QoL, independent living, social participation, and perceived safety between the intervention group (receiving Atlantis + Constable access) and the control group (receiving usual care).
  3. Develop free, open-source implementation guidelines and tools for local governments, housing associations, and community disability organizations to scale both interventions nationally.

Methodology

Phase 1: Co-Design & Intervention Refinement (Months 1–6)

Recruit 50 Lived Experience Advisors, stratified by disability type, urban/rural location, age, gender, race, and socioeconomic status, to participate in iterative co-design activities:

  • Atlantis Refinement: Focus groups and one-on-one user testing to expand platform features, including:
    • Modular sensory modulation tools for neurodivergent users (automatic adjustment of lighting, sound, and temperature)
    • Adaptive voice and gesture control for non-verbal and motor-impaired users
    • Low-bandwidth functionality for rural households with limited internet access
    • Full interoperability with existing assistive devices (e.g., power chair lifts, AAC devices)
  • Constable Refinement: Co-design of the peer-led framework, including:
    • Training curricula for Accessibility Constables on disability justice, reasonable accommodation advocacy, and de-escalation
    • A mobile tool for real-time accessibility reporting, peer navigation matching, and direct connection to a local Constable for in-person or virtual support during public outings
    • Community-led accountability systems to ensure Constables center disabled user autonomy

Phase 2: Randomized Controlled Trial (Months 7–21)

Recruit 200 disabled participants (100 urban, 100 rural) who report unmet independent living or access needs. Randomize 1:1 to intervention or control groups:

  • Intervention Group: Receive free Atlantis installation in their home and full access to the Constable framework for 12 months
  • Control Group: Receive usual care and standard assistive technology referrals for 12 months, with access to Atlantis and Constable at the end of the study as compensation
Outcome measures will be administered at baseline, 6 months, and 12 months:
  • WHOQOL-BREF (quality of life measure, adapted for disabled populations)
  • Independent Living Scale (measures ability to complete activities of daily living without external support)
  • Social Participation Scale (measures frequency of community and social engagement)
  • Perceived Access Safety Inventory (measures distress related to public space access barriers)
Qualitative data will be collected via monthly check-ins and semi-structured interviews with 40 purposively sampled participants at 12 months to explore lived experiences of the interventions.

Phase 3: Analysis & Toolkit Development (Months 22–24)

Quantitative analysis will use linear mixed-effects models to compare outcome changes between groups, controlling for demographic and intersectional covariates. Qualitative analysis will use critical disability theory-informed thematic analysis to center user perspectives. A free, open-source implementation toolkit will be developed to support scaling of Atlantis and Constable for non-research use.

Ethical Considerations

  • All research activities are led and co-governed by disabled researchers and Lived Experience Advisors to avoid ableist bias.
  • Informed consent processes are adapted to all communication needs: easy read formats, BSL interpretation, audio consent, and visual aids are provided.
  • All participants and Lived Experience Advisors are compensated at 1.5x the UK Living Wage to address systemic barriers to disabled people’s participation in research.
  • The Atlantis platform includes no surveillance features; all data collection is opt-in, and user data is fully anonymized and GDPR-compliant.
  • Constable conduct is overseen by a community-led accountability board to prevent misuse of authority.
  • Participants may withdraw from the study at any time without impact to their existing care or support services.

Project Timeline

Phase Months Key Activities
1: Co-Design & Refinement 1–6 Recruit Lived Experience Advisors; co-design Atlantis features; finalize Constable training curricula and mobile tool
2: RCT Implementation 7–12 Recruit RCT participants; install Atlantis for intervention group; train initial 100 Accessibility Constables; administer 6-month outcome measures
2: RCT Implementation 13–21 Deliver ongoing Constable support; conduct monthly check-ins; administer 12-month outcome measures; complete semi-structured interviews
3: Analysis & Dissemination 22–24 Analyze quantitative and qualitative data; develop open-source Atlantis codebase and Constable implementation toolkit; disseminate findings to policymakers and community groups

Expected Outcomes & Impact

  • Intervention group will demonstrate a 40% improvement in QoL scores, 35% reduction in unmet care needs, and 50% increase in social participation relative to the control group.
  • The Atlantis platform will be released as open-source, low-cost software adaptable for social housing, low-income households, and supported living settings.
  • The Constable framework will be adopted by 3 Scottish local authorities by the end of the project, with 200 trained Accessibility Constables serving 10,000+ disabled community members.
  • 10 peer-reviewed publications, 5 accessible community reports, and 2 policy briefings for the UK Department for Work and Pensions and EU Disability Rights Directorate to inform national access policy.

Budget Summary

Budget Category Cost (£) Details
Research Staff 520,000 Disability studies researchers, tech developers, Lived Experience Coordinator, 24 months of salary
Participant & Advisor Compensation 180,000 Living wage payments for 50 Advisors and 200 RCT participants, travel and accessibility costs
Atlantis Hardware & Software 240,000 Smart home devices for 100 intervention households, open-source platform development
Constable Training & Tool Development 140,000 Training for 200 Accessibility Constables, mobile tool development
Dissemination & Contingency 120,000 Accessible report production, community workshops, 10% contingency fund
Total 1,200,000
```

Lila’s seventh birthday came wrapped in sun-warmed cardboard and grandma’s sparkly wrapping paper, and inside sat Blueberry: a powder-blue two-wheeler with streamers the color of rainbow spaghetti, a wicker basket stitched with a daisy, and a bell that went ping-ping-ping so loud the sparrow nesting in the oak tree flew off when Lila rang it the first time.

All the kids on Maple Street zoomed past her house after school, popsicle juice dripping down their wrists, their own two-wheelers leaving wiggly chalk marks on the pavement. Lila sat on her porch step every afternoon, twisting Blueberry’s streamers around her fingers, her tummy full of fluttery ladybugs whenever she thought about climbing onto the seat.

The first sunny Saturday after her birthday, Dad dragged a tub of sidewalk chalk out to the driveway and said they’d take it slow. He knelt to adjust the seat so Lila’s toes just brushed the pavement when she sat, then held the back of Blueberry’s seat so tight his knuckles turned pale. “Left pedal first, then right,” he said, soft as a dandelion puff. “Just go at snail pace, okay?”

Lila climbed on, gripping the handlebars so tight her palms left little sweat marks on the rubber. She pushed the left pedal down, then the right, and for two whole seconds everything felt perfect—until her weight tilted left, and Blueberry swerved straight into the clover patch by the rose bush. Thorns snagged the hem of her overalls, and a tiny scrape bloomed on her elbow, pink as a strawberry. She plopped down in the grass, crossed her arms, and announced she’d stick to her scooter forever. Scooters never dumped you into rose bushes.

That’s when Crumble showed up. Crumble was the chonky orange stray that hung around Lila’s porch, stealing goldfish crackers from her picnic plate and napping in her rain boot. She trotted over, rubbed her fuzzy head on Lila’s scraped elbow, then hopped up on the low stone wall at the end of the driveway, curled her tail around her paws, and blinked like she was waiting for a show.

Lila followed her gaze, and her eyes went wide. Growing right by the mailbox at the end of the block was the biggest dandelion puff she’d ever seen, bigger than her whole fist, fluffy as a cloud. The wind had started to pick up, swirling the cherry blossom petals off the tree next to it, and Lila knew if she didn’t get to that dandelion soon, all its tiny seeds would blow away to the next town over.

She pushed herself up, brushed the clover leaves off her overalls, and marched back to Blueberry. “Hold the seat again?” she asked Dad, and he nodded, grinning.

This time, Lila didn’t squeeze the handlebars so hard. She wiggled her toes on the pavement once, took a deep breath that smelled like cut grass and cherry blossoms, and pushed the left pedal down, then the right, then the left again. The wind caught her streamers, making them flap like tiny rainbow flags, and the bell pinged when she hit a tiny bump in the driveway. She kept her eyes on that big fluffy dandelion, leaning just a tiny bit when Blueberry tilted, like she was dancing with it.

When she glanced over her shoulder to make sure Crumble was still watching, her breath caught. Dad was all the way back by the porch, leaning against the railing with his phone in his hand, grinning so big his dimples showed. He’d let go of the seat almost a full minute earlier.

For half a second, her tummy did a backflip, and Blueberry wobbled a little. But then she looked back at the dandelion, leaned just a hair to the right, and straightened right out. She glided all the way down the driveway, over the crack where ants marched back and forth, past the stone wall where Crumble sat up straight and meowed, and skidded to a stop right next to the mailbox.

She plucked the dandelion, cupped it in both hands, and took the biggest breath of her whole life. When she blew, hundreds of tiny seeds swirled around her, catching the sun like tiny bits of starlight. Crumble jumped off the wall and pounced after one seed that drifted toward the sidewalk, rolling in the grass like a fuzzy orange tornado.

Dad ran down the driveway and lifted her into a hug, spinning her around so her overalls flapped. “I saw!” he said, laughing. “You didn’t even look like you were thinking about it!”

That evening, Lila tucked her stuffed rabbit, Floppy, into Blueberry’s basket, and zipped back and forth along Maple Street, stopping every few feet to pluck a dandelion puff for the kids sitting on their porches. Crumble trotted right next to her the whole time, like her tiny orange bodyguard, meowing whenever Lila rang her bell.

When she climbed into bed that night, she found a tiny dandelion seed stuck in her braid, and she tucked it into the pocket of her overalls, already excited for the next sunny day.

we sit on the curb outside the laundromat
our laundry tumbling in a machine that smells
like someone else’s lavender fabric softener
barnet picks at the chipped black polish on their left thumb
the same thumb that bears the pale silver scar
from the time they tried to kickflip off the library curb
at sixteen, when we ditched study hall
to share a single blue raspberry slushie
same as today

they still buy the slushies too sweet
still leave the wrapper crumpled in the cup holder
of their beat up honda that smells like pine air freshener
and the half-eaten bag of sour patch kids
they keep under the seat for emergencies
they still can’t parallel park to save their life
will circle the block three times instead of trying
then grin and say “saved you the trouble”
when you huff and slide behind the wheel

last month when i cried on their couch
for three hours straight because my cat ran away
they didn’t say it would be okay
didn’t give me the stupid speech about things working out
they just handed me a spoon and a carton of mint chip
drew little t-rexes on every napkin in the house
and stayed up until two helping me tape flyers

Write a story about a man who is trying to get his life together. Put the name of the story in double angular brackets, i.e. <<story of xyz>>.

<<The 7:02 AM Coffee Run>>
Leo’s fridge is scrawled with neon green marker, three bullet points at the top of the white door, no fancy font, no lofty five-year plan: 1) Don’t hit snooze. 2) Drop Lila’s volcano at Clara’s before school. 3) Submit the branding contract draft by 9 AM.
It’s 6:47 AM, and he’s already passed the first test. Three months prior, he’d have hit snooze four times, woken up at 10 AM to a string of missed texts from his ex-wife and a half-empty IPA on the coffee table, the ghost of the bender that made him miss his daughter’s 10th birthday. That day, Clara had sent one text, sharp as broken glass: She waited for you. I’m done letting her be disappointed. It had been the thing that pried him off the couch, that made him call his old college roommate who’d gotten sober five years prior, that got him to his first AA meeting in a church basement where the coffee tasted like burnt cardboard and no one cared that he cried through his entire share.
Today is day 62. The 30-day chip in his jacket pocket is chipped on the edge, from when he tripped over a fire hydrant leaving a meeting last week, and he runs his thumb over the nick as he yanks open the hall closet to grab his backpack.
The volcano tips first.
Lila had left it at his place last weekend, papier-mâché cone painted neon orange, a little baggie of baking soda tucked into the crater, sticky with glitter she’d dumped on it “for extra drama.” It hits the floor hard, the baggie splitting, baking soda dust blooming over his laptop, his notebook, the stack of resume drafts he’d been avoiding for weeks.
For half a second, the old Leo rears up: the one that would have screamed, kicked the closet door, grabbed the half-empty can of IPA he’d forgotten he stashed under the sink six weeks prior, and texted Clara that he was sick, sorry, couldn’t make it. He can almost taste the bitter fizz of it, almost feel the numbness rolling in to swallow the panic.
But this Leo grabs a paper towel off the counter first, then fumbles for his phone to text his sponsor, Marty, before he even thinks about the beer under the sink. Volcano broke. Baking soda everywhere, he types. Marty texts back 30 seconds later: Scoop it up. Duct tape the cone. Lila won’t care if it’s lumpy.
He’s right. Leo scoops the baking soda back into a snack baggie, tapes the crumpled cone back together, leaves a streak of glitter on his cheek in the process. It’s lopsided, the orange paint smudged in one spot, but it’s still a volcano. He shoves it back into his backpack, grabs his keys, and runs out the door before he can overthink it.
The 7:02 AM bus is idling at the stop when he rounds the corner, breath coming in cold March fog, his sneakers slapping the wet sidewalk. He hauls himself up the steps, fumbles for his bus pass, and collapses into a seat by the window, the volcano propped carefully on his lap.
His phone buzzes. It’s Javi, his old drinking buddy, the one he used to play poker with every Friday until he got sober. Dude, poker night tonight, the text reads. Got your favorite IPA on ice. Come through, we miss your terrible bluffs.
Leo stares at the text for a full minute. He can picture Javi’s basement, the blue string lights, the crinkle of chip bags, the burn of IPA going down his throat, the way he’d forget about Lila and Clara and the graphic design job he lost when his startup folded, and all the ways he’d fucked up, if only for a few hours.
Then he pulls up the photo he has set as his lock screen: Lila dusted in that same sparkly volcano glitter, grinning on his couch, holding up the papier-mâché cone like a trophy. He texts back: Not tonight. Got a meeting, and I’m taking Lila for pizza after her science fair tomorrow. Then he mutes the group chat, shoves his phone back in his pocket, and pulls out his laptop to tweak the contract draft.
He gets to Clara’s townhouse at 7:38, two minutes early. She opens the door in her work blazer, her hair pulled back in a bun, her expression guarded—like she’s waiting for him to say he messed up, that the volcano is gone, that he forgot again.
“Hi,” he says, holding out the lopsided volcano. “Baking soda spilled a little, but I refilled it. It’s a little beat up, but Lila said she wanted it to look like a real volcano that had erupted before, right?”
Clara blinks, like she didn’t expect him to remember that throwaway line Lila had mumbled mid-cartoon marathon two weeks prior. She takes the volcano carefully, then glances at the glitter on his cheek, and huffs a small, surprised laugh. “She did. Thanks.” She pauses, then steps back inside and grabs a black travel mug off the counter, hands it to him. “It’s your usual. No cream, no sugar. Good luck with the contract.”
He doesn’t get to say anything before Lila comes barrelling down the stairs, her sparkly rain boots thudding against the hardwood, and launches herself into his chest. She hugs him so tight his ribs ache, her hair smelling like strawberry shampoo, and she mumbles into his jacket: “I thought you’d forget.”
“I’m done forgetting the stuff that matters,” he says, and it doesn’t feel like a flimsy promise he’s going to break, the way all his old ones had. It feels like something he can do, one small thing at a time.
He walks to the coffee shop two blocks over, the travel mug warm in his hand, and sits at a corner booth by the window. He pulls up the contract draft, reads it one more time, hits send at 7:58 AM, ten minutes early.
He pulls out his neon green marker, leans over the table, and writes tomorrow’s three things on a napkin, neat and plain, no fanfare: 1) Bring extra baking soda to the science fair. 2) Drop off the first payment for the car repair. 3) Call Mom.
Then he takes a sip of coffee, hot and bitter and perfect, and watches the sun come up over the streetlights. He’s 62 days sober. He’s got a freelance gig that might turn into a full-time job. His daughter still wants to hug him. It’s not perfect. It’s not the grand, put-together life he thought he’d have at 38, with a white picket fence and a corner office and no chipped sobriety chips or lopsided papier-mâché volcanoes. But it’s his, and it’s a start.

**Subject: 🎶 Urgent (very good) album rec to fix your stale study playlist**

Hi Luheng!
Hope your organic chem midterm cramming isn’t making you pull 3 AM energy drink all-nighters again (if it is, I’m dropping off a matcha latte and your favorite matcha Pocky at your lab tomorrow at 2 PM, no arguments allowed). I remembered you complaining on our grocery run last week that your entire study playlist is just the same 12 Phoebe Bridgers songs on loop, and you’re this close to crying every time “Kyoto” comes on? I have the exact fix.

It’s an album called *Lilith* that I stumbled on last month, and I haven’t gone a single day without listening to it front to back at least once. First off, it’s tailor-made for your taste: it’s a collaborative project from 11 female and non-binary indie artists (Julien Baker has a feature, Adrianne Lenker co-wrote two tracks—you already know that’s a win) built around the myth of Lilith, the first wife of Adam who left Eden rather than be subservient. You know how you were geeking out over that feminist mythology paper you wrote last semester about pre-Abrahamic desert goddesses? This entire album is basically that, but set to music that swings from soft, gut-punch acoustic folk to glitchy, ethereal electropop. Zero skips. I promise.

I’ll even curate your first listen order if you don’t have 45 minutes for a full run-through right now:
1. Start with “Eve’s Reply” first—it’s the opening track, with that quiet, brooding vocal harmony you love that sounds like it’s being sung in a stone church. I swear the first time I heard the chorus I had to pull over on my bike because I got full-body chills.
2. If you need something with a beat for your 20-minute commute to lab? Put on “Wings in the Subway”—it’s snappy, has a little bass line that makes you walk faster, and the lyrics about feeling like an otherworldly weirdo just trying to buy eggs hit so hard for our 9 AM hungover grocery runs.
3. Save “Covenant” for when you’re up late grading those undergrad lab reports and you’re tired and over it. It’s a slow, haunting piano ballad about choosing your own people over the rules you were raised with, and it made me cry the first three times I listened to it. No shame.

<<The Wrong Print>>
Lila Marlow is a rookie forensic technician working for the Chicago PD. She lives alone and spends most of her free time volunteering at a free medical clinic for unhoused and low income people.
Jax Reed is a small time con artist who relies on fake IDs to pull off low stakes identity theft. He visits the same free clinic every month to pick up free asthma inhalers and cancer medication for his younger sister. He cannot afford either medication on his own.
The clinic rolls out a new biometric check in system to prevent people from picking up medications for others. The system uses a special nanotech gel to capture clear fingerprint data for each visitor. The clinic bought the gel in bulk from a discount supplier to cut costs. The supplier had skipped critical safety testing to meet the order deadline.
One rainy Tuesday Lila and Jax check in within thirty seconds of each other. Lila presses her full hand to the gel coated scan pad first. Her skin sheds RNA fragments that stick to the leftover gel on the pad. Jax presses his full hand to the same pad right after her. The faulty gel transfers Lila’s ridge pattern RNA to his skin. His own RNA also transfers to the remaining gel on the pad. A clinic volunteer wipes the pad clean right after Jax finishes his scan. Neither person notices anything out of the ordinary.
A week later Lila processes a fingerprint from a gas station robbery. The print matches her own right index finger perfectly. She panics because she has no memory of being at that gas station. She double checks her lab equipment. She runs the scan three more times. Every result comes back identical to her official print on file with the department.
That same day Jax tries to use his fake ID to pick up a refill of his sister’s medication at a local pharmacy. The pharmacy uses fingerprint verification to prevent fraud. The scanner pulls up Lila Marlow’s name and employment information instead of his fake ID details. Jax freezes. He runs out of the pharmacy before any staff can question him.
Lila starts digging into the clinic she volunteers at. She pulls the check in logs for the day she got her annual flu shot. She tracks Jax down to a small hostel on the west side of the city. She confronts him outside the building’s front door. Jax immediately recognizes her face from the pharmacy lookup screen.
They both compare their fingerprints side by side on Lila’s portable work scanner. They find every single one of their ten fingers has swapped patterns. Lila tests a sample of the leftover gel from the clinic. She confirms the faulty formula caused the permanent swap. She also realizes Jax has been using his new print to sneak into office buildings and steal small electronics over the past week. All the building security scanners flag the prints as belonging to a city employee so no one stops him. He says he only stole the items to pay for his sister’s upcoming surgery.
A detective from Lila’s department calls her that night. They found her print on a broken window at a downtown tech startup that was robbed the night before. They want her to come in for questioning immediately. Lila knows she will lose her job and face felony charges if she cannot prove someone else has her fingerprints.
Jax offers to make a deal. He will turn over all the stolen goods and confess to all the robberies if Lila helps him get a spot in the city’s work release program instead of jail time. Lila hesitates. She remembers meeting Jax’s sister at the clinic. She remembers bringing the girl extra fruit snacks during her last chemotherapy appointment. She agrees to the deal.
They go to the police station together the next morning. They bring the leftover gel from the clinic as evidence. They bring the supplier’s internal report that admits the gel was never safety tested. The department runs independent tests on both Lila and Jax. They confirm the fingerprint swap is real. The department drops all charges against Lila. They agree to give Jax a work release position doing maintenance at police headquarters if he completes all his court ordered community service.
Six months later Lila gets promoted to lead forensic technician for her department. She helped write new city wide safety protocols for all biometric scanning equipment. Jax works full time as a maintenance worker at the police station. He uses his steady paychecks to pay for his sister’s surgery and physical therapy. They meet for pancakes every Saturday morning at the diner down the street from the free clinic. They still have each other’s fingerprints. They joke about being the only two people in the city who can unlock each other’s phones. They both volunteer at the clinic every other weekend. They help run the new medication pickup program for families who cannot afford care.

"5-Day Mesa, Arizona Itinerary
Day 1: Downtown Mesa Arrival & Cultural Exploration
Kick off your trip by taking the light rail from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport to downtown Mesa, a quick 25-minute ride that lets you skip rental car lines and soak in early views of the Valley. Check into a cozy local boutique hotel like the Mesa Downtown Courtyard, then grab frothy lattes and flaky almond croissants at Loom Coffee Co., a beloved neighborhood spot with a sunlit back patio. Wander the lively Main Street corridor, stopping to look at vibrant murals by local Indigenous and Latinx artists, pop into tiny independent bookstores, and grab a casual lunch at Liberty Market, a farm-to-table staple that sources produce from nearby family farms. Later that afternoon, explore the Mesa Arts Center, the largest multidisciplinary arts campus in the state, where you can learn about the city’s creative legacy, browse free contemporary art exhibits, or lounge in the leafy central courtyard dotted with desert succulents. End your day with dinner at the Lumberyard Brewing Co. taproom, sipping crisp local lagers and sharing loaded nachos under luminous string lights strung over their dog-friendly patio.
Day 2: Red Rock Hiking & Indigenous History
Lace up your sturdiest hiking boots and head 20 minutes east to Usery Mountain Regional Park at sunrise, when the desert air is cool and the red rock buttes glow soft gold. Tackle the moderate 3-mile Wind Cave Trail, which winds through saguaro stands to a shaded cave opening with panoramic views of the Superstition Mountains. Pack a light picnic with fresh citrus, local date bars, and cold lemon water to enjoy at the trailhead, then make your way to Mesa Grande Cultural Park, a 1,000-year-old Hohokam village site with a massive ancient platform mound. Join a free ranger-led tour to learn about the Hohokam’s innovative irrigation systems and the living legacy of Indigenous communities in the region, then wander the marked paths lined with interpretive signs. For dinner, swing by Los Dos Molinos, a laid-back family-owned Mexican spot famous for its smoky chiles rellenos and tangy lime margaritas that pack a gentle kick.
Day 3: Family-Friendly Fun & Outdoor Entertainment
Start your morning at the Arizona Museum of Natural History, a kid-favorite spot where little ones (and curious adults) will love roaming the dinosaur fossil halls, walking through a simulated 16th-century Hohokam pueblo, and panning for real gold in the outdoor mining exhibit. Grab a quick lunch at the museum’s casual café, then head to Dana Park Village Square, a leafy open-air shopping center with dozens of local boutiques, name-brand retailers, and charming dessert spots. Stop for a scoop of lavender honey ice cream at the local creamery, then browse handcrafted jewelry and desert-themed art at the on-site artisan market. Later that evening, catch a live show at the Mesa Amphitheatre, a beloved outdoor venue that hosts everything from stand-up comedy sets to classic rock cover bands. Lay out a soft blanket on the lawn, grab a bucket of cold beer, and enjoy the cool desert night air as the stars come out.

# Cover Letter (For the Barista Opening at Maple & Bean Coffee Co.)
October 12, 2024

To the team that refills the front porch dog bowl
before the first streetlight fades,
that tapes third-grade dinosaur drawings
next to the yoga class flyers on the community board—

I’m the girl who’s occupied the corner window table
every other Saturday for six months,
sipping your house-made lavender latte
and scribbling bad poetry,
watching you laugh with Mr. Henderson
when he forgets he already paid for his black coffee.
Today I’m not just here for caffeine—
I’m here to ask to join the team.

First: I’ve got *2 years crafting lattes for early commuters*
at the corner gas station shop across town—
I know the rhythm of the 6am rush:
the construction crews yelling for double shots,
the college students begging for extra syrup
before their 8am midterms,
the quiet hush of the widows who come in
just to sit and watch the rain for an hour.

I’m proud to say I *memorized 17 regulars’ orders at my last barista gig*
before I’d worked there a month—
Mabel, who wanted extra foam, no nutmeg,
Javier, who got a cold brew with a splash of chocolate milk
for his 10-year-old on weekends,
Ms. Lee, who only wanted hot water and a lemon slice
but always left a $5 tip just for chatting.
I know regulars aren’t just transactions—
they’re the heart of a shop like this.

I’m *first-aid certified for scraped knees and oat milk spills*
— I’ve patched up a toddler who tripped over a power cord
and mopped up a half-gallon of oat milk
before it could seep under the pastry case,
all without making a single customer wait
longer than 3 minutes for their drink.
I don’t panic when the rush hits;
I just tie my apron tighter and keep pouring.

For what it’s worth, I *can carry 3 stacked pastry trays without crumbing a scone*
— I tested it last week, actually,
when I helped your Sunday barista restock the case
after a rush of post-church customers.
I know your lemon scones are the best in the county,
and I’d never let a crumb go to waste,
or let a customer get a sad, squished croissant
on my watch.

And I *write tiny doodles on cup lids for shy kids*
— cats mostly, sometimes dinosaurs,
once a very lopsided unicorn that a little girl
taped to her fridge for three months,
her mom told me later.
I know a coffee shop isn’t just about coffee;
it’s about the little things that make a hard day
feel a little softer.

I don’t want to work at a chain where I have to upsell
protein boxes or call every customer “partner.”
I want to work here, where the syrup is stirred in the back,
where the owner brings her golden retriever to work on Tuesdays,
where the music is always 90s folk and no one yells if you
sing along a little too loud while you steam milk.
I want to be part of the thing that makes this neighborhood
feel like home.

I can start as early as next week,
I’ve got my own tamper and a pair of non-slip shoes
that don’t squeak on tile,
and I’m happy to come in for a trial shift any morning before 10am
so you can see me work before you decide.
You can reach me at (555) 123-4567,
or leave a note for me under the corner window table
if I’m not around.

Thank you for considering me—
even if you don’t hire me, I’ll still be back
for the lavender lattes and the dinosaur drawings on the wall.
Sincerely,
Lila Marlow

The line “Coincidence is God's way of remaining anonymous” wraps around a universal human urge to find meaning in the unplanned intersections of life. It does not demand adherence to any specific religious doctrine or narrow vision of the divine. It instead speaks to the quiet sense of wonder that rises in most people when they encounter a moment that feels too perfectly aligned to write off as pure random chance. I first felt the weight of this idea when I was 22 years old just a few months after my grandma died. She had been the person who taught me to love poetry and she had left me her tattered 40 year old copy of Mary Oliver’s selected works filled with her handwritten notes in the margins and pressed wildflowers between the pages. I carried that book everywhere for weeks after her funeral. I brought it with me on a work trip to a city I had never visited before three states away from the small town where she had lived her entire life. I left it on a public bus on my last day in that city. I searched the lost and found for hours and I cried in the bus station parking lot because I thought I had lost the last physical piece of her that felt truly hers.
Three months later I was sitting in a coffee shop in my own hometown waiting for a friend to arrive for brunch. A woman I had never seen before sat down at the table next to mine and pulled out a tattered blue poetry book with the exact same worn cover as my grandma’s copy. I leaned over almost without thinking to ask where she had gotten it. She flipped open the cover to show me the name my grandma had written there in her loopy cursive handwriting. The woman had found the book on that same bus three months prior. She had seen the name written inside and noticed it matched the first name of her own late mother. She had carried it with her every day since then hoping she would somehow run into someone who knew the owner. She was only in my town for a single day for a work conference that had been scheduled at the last minute. That interaction stopped me in my tracks. I did not walk away believing I had witnessed a grand supernatural miracle or that a humanoid God in the sky had personally arranged for that book to find its way back to me. But I did walk away feeling like there was some soft invisible thread weaving through the small unscripted moments of life that we rarely take the time to notice.
Modern culture often pushes us to force every moment into one of two neat boxes. We are taught to label things either meaningless random chance or intentional deliberate design. We live in a world that prioritizes control and predictability and data above almost everything else. We map out our career paths five years in advance. We create detailed budgets for every dollar we earn. We use algorithms to sort through potential romantic partners to find the exact right fit. We want to know exactly why things happen exactly when they happen. We hate the mess of uncertainty. When something occurs that does not fit into our carefully constructed systems of cause and effect we rush to dismiss it as a fluke or elevate it to a divine sign. This quote pushes back against that rigid binary. It offers a third way to engage with the world. It suggests that the divine or whatever name we choose to give to the unnameable connectedness of all life does not operate in grand obvious ways that demand attention or worship. It operates through the small quiet moments that could so easily be brushed off if we are not paying attention.
Anonymity is the core of the idea’s power. If the divine made its presence obvious every time it touched a person’s life those moments would lose their soft magic. People would start to treat them as transactions. They would perform goodness or piety in the hopes of earning more favorable coincidences. They would stop living fully in the present because they would be too busy scanning the horizon for clear undeniable signs. They would feel entitled to intervention instead of grateful for the small gifts that appear when we least expect them. Anonymity lets the work of connection happen without fanfare without pressure without the weight of human expectation. Imagine if every perfectly timed text from a friend right when you were about to break down was clearly labeled as a divine act. People would start to see those texts as rewards instead of gestures of love between two people. They would stop reaching out to their friends just because they thought of them and start doing it only when they wanted something in return.
Even people who do not believe in any God at all can find deep truth in this quote. For atheists or agnostics the “God” in the line can be redefined as the collective web of human connection as the quiet unseen logic of the universe as the way our own subconscious minds draw us to people and places and experiences that we need even when we do not know we need them. An atheist who runs into an old childhood friend on a remote hiking trail thousands of miles from where they both grew up can still feel that spark of wonder that comes from the unplanned collision of two separate lives. They can still recognize that there is a beauty to those moments that goes beyond the cold math of statistical probability. The quote does not require religious faith to resonate. It only requires a willingness to slow down enough to notice the small strange beautiful overlaps that make up so much of our daily lives.
Critics of the idea might point to the painful coincidences that cause harm and suffering. They might ask if a person who runs into their abusive ex partner at a grocery store after years of no contact is seeing God’s anonymous work. They might ask if a person who misses a life saving medical appointment because their car broke down is experiencing the same quiet design. The quote does not promise that all coincidences are good or kind or gentle. It does not claim that every unplanned moment holds an obvious positive purpose that we can see right away. It only suggests that unplanned moments carry weight that we often ignore if we are too focused on our own plans. Even the hard coincidences can lead us to places we need to go even if we cannot see that at the time. The run in with an ex might force a person to confront unresolved trauma they had been avoiding for years. The missed medical appointment might lead a person to get a second opinion from a different doctor that catches a condition the first provider missed. That does not mean the pain of those moments is not real or valid. It just means that even the hard unplanned parts of life are not empty of meaning if we choose to look for it.
This quote is ultimately an invitation to live more openly and more curiously. It invites us to stop seeing the world as a series of random unrelated events that happen to us. It invites us to stop trying to control every single part of our lives down to the smallest detail. It invites us to pause when we encounter a strange aligned moment and hold space for wonder instead of rushing to explain it away. It also invites us to recognize that we can be the anonymous hand of that larger connectedness for other people. The woman who found my grandma’s book did not know she was part of a moment that would stay with me for the rest of my life. She was just being a decent person carrying a book she found hoping to return it to its rightful owner. That is the beauty of the anonymity. We all get to be part of those small meaningful moments for each other without even knowing it. We do not have to be famous or powerful or religiously devout to be a vessel for that quiet connection. We just have to show up and pay attention and be open to the unplanned parts of life that end up being the most memorable and the most meaningful of all. We spend so much of our time chasing big defined markers of success that we often overlook the tiny unplanned moments that shape us the most. The stranger who holds the door for you when your hands are full. The song that comes on the radio right when you needed to hear those exact lyrics. The rainstorm that cancels your outdoor plans and leads you to stay home and meet your new neighbor who becomes your chosen family. These are the moments that make life feel rich and full and connected. This quote reminds us that we do not need to have all the answers to appreciate that magic. We just need to be willing to see it even when it does not call attention to itself.

As a 12th grader navigating college applications alongside senior year classes, extracurriculars, and all the chaos of your final year of high school, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed—but breaking the process into intentional, actionable steps will help you submit your strongest possible profile without burning out. Here’s targeted advice tailored to your needs:
First, build a balanced, manageable school list to avoid spreading yourself too thin. Aim for 2-3 safeties (schools where your GPA and test scores fall well above the admitted middle 50%, and you’d genuinely be excited to attend, not just view as a fallback), 3-4 targets (schools where your stats align perfectly with the admitted middle 50%), and 1-2 reaches (dream schools where your stats are below the middle 50% but you have a standout hook, like unique extracurricular impact or a personal story). Cap your total applications at 8—15+ rushed, generic submissions will never be stronger than 8 thoughtful, customized ones.
Next, craft a personal statement that feels authentically you, not a cliché. Skip overdone topics like sports championship wins or short mission trips unless you can anchor the essay to a tiny, specific moment that reveals your core values. For example, instead of writing about winning a state debate award, write about the 10 minutes before every round where you taped a photo of your grandma’s immigration paperwork to your laptop to remind you why you advocate for equitable education policy. Prioritize showing, not telling: describe the frustration of staying up until 1am fixing your robotics team’s broken prototype instead of just stating “I’m resilient.” Have two people review your essay: one who knows you well (like a favorite teacher or mentor) to confirm it sounds true to your voice, and one who doesn’t know you well (like a school counselor or family friend outside your inner circle) to make sure your core message comes through without extra context.
For supplemental essays, never use generic templates—admissions officers can spot a reused essay instantly. Before writing any supplement, spend 10 minutes deep diving the school’s website to learn their core values, signature programs, recent campus initiatives, or student-run clubs that align with your interests. Avoid vague lines like “I love your beautiful campus” or “your prestigious faculty” that could apply to any school. Instead, write something specific: “I’m eager to join UW-Madison’s Campus Food Justice Collective, which aligns with my two years running my high school’s free pantry for food-insecure students, and I hope to build on that work through their Sustainable Food Systems minor.” This proves you’re not just spamming applications—you actually want to join that specific campus community.
When requesting letters of recommendation, skip the teacher who gave you an A but barely interacts with you. Opt for 11th grade (the most recent upper-level) teachers you’ve built a genuine relationship with: the English teacher who stayed after class to discuss your creative writing, the AP Gov teacher who advised your student voter registration club. Give them at least 4 weeks of notice, and attach a “brag sheet” with specific memories from their class, your core values, and your post-high school goals to give them concrete details to highlight, instead of forcing them to write a generic, vague letter. If a school allows an optional extra recommendation, ask a coach, boss, or community mentor to showcase a side of you that doesn’t come through in academic recs—like how you trained your 6-person café staff on new POS systems as a part-time shift lead.
Use the additional information section strategically, not as an extra essay. If you had a grade dip, family hardship, or gap in extracurriculars, explain it briefly and factually, no drama: “My junior year first semester GPA dipped from a 3.9 to a 3.2 while my dad underwent open heart surgery, and I took on 20 hours a week of childcare for my two younger siblings; I earned a 4.0 the following semester once he recovered.” If you’re applying test-optional, only submit scores if they fall at or above the school’s admitted middle 50%—there’s no penalty for going test-optional at nearly all U.S. schools, so don’t waste time retaking the SAT/ACT if your scores won’t strengthen your profile.
Finally, stay organized to avoid last-minute mistakes. Make a master spreadsheet with every school’s deadline, required materials (transcripts, test scores, recs), supplemental essay prompts, and submission status. Set calendar alerts for 1 week, 3 days, and 24 hours before each deadline, and submit at least 48 hours early to avoid server crashes, last-minute typos, or missed requirements. For your activities section, prioritize depth over breadth: list 5-7 activities you’ve spent consistent time on, and quantify your impact whenever possible—instead of “member of environmental club,” write “Led 4 school-wide recycling drives that diverted 2,100 pounds of waste, secured $1,600 in local business grants to install 10 water bottle filling stations, and grew campus refill usage by 40% in one school year.”
You cannot fail with the steps listed above.

"This RUBRIC is designed to assess original musical compositions across all genres, from solo acoustic works to full orchestral pieces, and is calibrated for both student creators and emerging professional composers. Every RUBRIC criterion is weighted to balance technical skill and artistic vision, ensuring no composer is penalized for experimenting with non-traditional structures or sound design. Before scoring, evaluators must review the full submitted score, any accompanying demo recording, and the composer’s artist statement to contextualize creative choices, as this RUBRIC prioritizes intentionality over rigid adherence to conventional musical rules.
***
The first weighted core criterion is MUSICAL COHERENCE, which accounts for 30% of the total RUBRIC score. To score highly in this category, a composition must have a clear throughline, whether that’s a recurring melodic motif, consistent harmonic logic, a deliberate emotional arc, or a conceptual throughline that unifies even dissonant or experimental sections. Low scores in this category are reserved for works that feel unstructured by accident (not intentional experimentation) or where transitions between sections feel arbitrary, with no clear connection to the composer’s stated artistic goal. Evaluators must note that MUSICAL COHERENCE does not require a traditional verse-chorus structure; ambient, free improvisation, and aleatoric works can earn full marks if their creative choices align with a unified vision.
***
The second core criterion is TECHNICAL PROFICIENCY, making up 25% of the total RUBRIC score. This category assesses the composer’s understanding of notation (if a score is submitted), instrumental or vocal ranges, voicing for ensembles, rhythmic clarity, and harmonic consistency relative to the work’s intended style. For electronic compositions, TECHNICAL PROFICIENCY also includes sound design quality, mixing balance, and intentional use of signal processing rather than accidental distortion or muddled audio. Evaluators are instructed not to penalize young or new composers for small notation errors, as long as the intended musical choice is clear; this RUBRIC distinguishes between avoidable mistakes and deliberate stylistic flourishes that break conventional rules.
***
The third core criterion is CREATIVE ORIGINALITY, which accounts for 20% of the total RUBRIC score. This category rewards works that bring a unique perspective to their genre, whether that’s reimagining a traditional folk form with modern production, blending disparate cultural musical influences with respect and intentionality, or introducing a novel melodic, rhythmic, or textural idea that feels fresh rather than derivative. Low scores in CREATIVE ORIGINALITY are only assigned when a composition directly lifts motifs or structures from existing works without attribution or transformative context, or when it relies so heavily on generic genre tropes that it lacks any distinct artistic voice. This RUBRIC explicitly celebrates risk-taking here, even if experimental choices do not land perfectly, as creative growth often stems from bold, untested ideas.
***
The fourth core criterion is PERFORMANCE FEASIBILITY, making up 15% of the total RUBRIC score. This category assesses whether the work is playable or performable by the intended musicians or ensemble, with reasonable rehearsal time and access to standard equipment. For example, a work written for a high school string quartet would lose marks if it includes extended techniques that require professional-level training not typical for that ensemble, unless the composer explicitly notes the work is intended for a specialized youth group with advanced training. For electronic or pre-recorded works, PERFORMANCE FEASIBILITY evaluates whether the work can be presented in the intended venue (e.g., a gallery installation piece that requires a specific 8-channel speaker setup will not be penalized if the composer clearly states that requirement in their submission materials). This RUBRIC recognizes that some composers write works for hypothetical or future performances, so evaluators should prioritize clarity of performance requirements over whether the work has already been staged.
***
The fifth and final core criterion is AUDIENCE ENGAGEMENT, which accounts for the remaining 10% of the total RUBRIC score. This category assesses the work’s ability to connect with its intended audience, whether that audience is a room of experimental noise fans, a family-friendly community concert crowd, or a panel of academic composition judges. A work that is intentionally alienating for thematic or artistic purposes can still earn full marks in this category if that effect aligns with the composer’s stated goal for their target audience. Evaluators must avoid imposing their personal taste on this category, instead judging AUDIENCE ENGAGEMENT relative to the work’s intended context and purpose. Overall, this RUBRIC is designed to uplift composers of all skill levels and stylistic backgrounds, providing actionable feedback that supports growth rather than just assigning a numerical score."
